title: Writing Is Thinking
author: James Traub
summary: James Traub, who runs a volunteer writing program in New York public high schools, argues that a coherent, systematic writing curriculum can develop the capacity for thought. He used to believe writing was a dependent variable of reading, but the Writing Revolution, developed by Judith Hochman, persuaded him that writing instruction can reverse that relationship. The method starts at the sentence, teaching students to expand it with conjunctions and appositives such as because, but, so and unless, and it grounds writing in the content of each class. He compares the step-by-step approach to phonics and cites the New Dorp High School turnaround, where explicit sentence instruction improved reading comprehension. He criticizes free writing as encouraging students to treat writing as physical self-expression, and warns that students who cannot write will be first to surrender to AI.
points: Writing is the public record of inner thought, and it is hard because thinking is hard, which makes unstructured free writing a poor substitute for instruction.
The Writing Revolution begins at the sentence and teaches students to expand it with connectives like because, but, so and unless that unlock complex structures.
Students who write fragments often cannot recognize conjunctions and appositives in reading, so explicit writing instruction can improve comprehension and start a virtuous cycle.
Writing should be grounded in curricular knowledge and taught in every class, not as an autonomous exercise in self-expression.
Students who cannot use writing for their own thoughts will be the first to hand it over to AI, so systematic writing instruction is also a defense of human thinking.
quotes: Writing is, in fact, the public record of one’s inner thought process; it’s hard because thinking is hard.

The exercises in “free writing” now rampant in schools encourage students to regard writing as a physical rather than a cognitive act, as if it required that one throw off the restraints of thought rather than apply them.
Hochman agrees on the centrality of planning and re-writing. And she argues, along with Hirsch and educational traditionalists, that writing must be grounded in curricular knowledge.
She observes that students write sentence fragments, or blunt declarative sentences, because they do not recognize the more complex structures embodied in a conjunction or an appositive phrase.
This extremely methodical, step-by-step process bears some analogy to phonics instruction, in which children learn, sometimes laboriously, to combine phonemes to form words.
The master key for reading is phonics. Nothing like that really exists for writing; schools typically substitute “self-expression” for genuine mastery.
The only way to save them is to make them unwilling to surrender the power of writing to a machine. That would, indeed, constitute a revolution.
